Share ‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe on social media
Members of the Russian delegation holds talks with their Ukrainian counterparts in negotiations mediated by the US in Abu Dhabi on November 10, 2026 [AFP]
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian drone struck a small house in the northern Ukrainian town of Hlukhiv, burying a nine-year-old boy and his grandmother under the debris.
Two Ukrainian police officers arrived on Saturday to dig them out, apply a tourniquet to the woman’s bleeding arm and take them away in their car.
But a second drone struck their vehicle, killing one of the officers, Mykola Savchenko, who covered the boy with his body, the Ministry of Internal Affairs said.
Such double-tap attacks are Ukraine’s daily reality as the war grinds on to its fifth anniversary. They’re also a metaphor for Russia’s latest attempts to target both Ukraine and those Kyiv has long hoped would help it survive Moscow’s onslaught – NATO and Europe.
On the surface, Russia is engaged in United States-mediated diplomacy. But Russian diplomats who met with US negotiators in Abu Dhabi for trilateral talks involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington last week presented demands that go far beyond any peace settlement.
Moscow hasn’t agreed to Kyiv’s proposal to freeze the war along the current front lines as Ukraine lacks Western missile interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles and jet drones.
Instead, the Kremlin has shifted the focus of talks from a ceasefire and peace to demands that, if accepted, could dismantle Europe’s post-Cold War security architecture, analysts said.
Russia wants NATO to withdraw its troops from Central and Eastern Europe and ban the bloc’s further expansion, according to leaked documents obtained by The New York Times, The Economist and several Ukrainian media outlets.
Moscow also wants to ink nonaggression pacts with individual European nations, something that may sound alluring to Russia’s neighbours, such as Estonia or Finland.
“Agreements of this kind could be reached, among other things, with individual NATO member states, which would then receive, for instance, additional individual security guarantees” from Moscow, Russian negotiator Alexey Drobinin said at a news conference after the Abu Dhabi talks.
But a string of such agreements could in effect negate NATO’s cornerstone principle to regard any armed attack against one member state as an attack against all of its 32 members.
“NATO will collapse, and European nations will [individually] be face to face with Russia,” said Boris Bondarev, a former Russian diplomat who left his Ministry of Foreign Affairs job in protest against Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Europe will surrender to Russia without firing a single shot in its defence, without losing a single soldier or spending a single shell,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Such individual deals are an absolutely blatant attempt to demolish Europe’s unity, which has already been bursting at the seams, and to undermine NATO’s unity,” said Bondarev, also the author of Time to Win the War, a book that tracks the potential steps needed to reach a peace agreement.
Any nonaggression pacts would most likely include conditions that bar a signatory nation from participating in a future conflict between Russia and another European nation, he said, destroying any potential for collective defence against Moscow.
Russia’s demands were presented to US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff but not to European leaders.
“Russians want to talk to Americans. They don’t want to talk to Europe,” Maria Kucherenko, executive director at the Strategic Intelligence Institute, a think tank in Kyiv, told Al Jazeera.
To Kucherenko, who has for years scrutinised Moscow’s negotiating tactics, the “maximalist” demands continue the Kremlin’s habit of asking for everything.
Russia’s “demands will be maximalist, the way they used to be, and they will be deceptive about the subsequence of steps [towards a peace deal] in their interests. They’ll put politics ahead of security, the way they’ve done all these years,” she said.
Kushner, a real estate developer and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, used the word “very” abundantly to describe the talks.
“These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” Kushner said at a news conference.
To Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Russia’s demands sound otherworldly.
Russian President Vladimir Putin “lives in a different reality”, Zelenskyy wrote on X on Wednesday, adding, “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true.”
“We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100 percent what they want,” Zelenskyy said at a news conference hours later.
A top Ukrainian negotiator decried the “difficulty” of the Abu Dhabi talks.
“This round of talks was one of the most difficult ones. I believe the Russians came with very strict instructions, so it was really hard to ease the discussions,” Davyd Arakhamia, who has taken part in each round of talks since 2022, said on Wednesday.
Stalling the talks will not just weaken Kyiv and demoralise Ukrainians, it may also help Russia buy time until it is politically stronger in Europe’s key nations.
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has pledged to phase out France’s military and financial aid to Ukraine within six months if she wins April’s presidential election. She is currently the frontrunner.
And if Germany’s ruling coalition falls apart amid debates over the budget, debt and economic stagnation, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is positioned to win a snap vote. It leads in national polls and is well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
AfD also wants to terminate aid to Ukraine, push for immediate peace talks with Moscow and lift sanctions so Germany can once again buy Russian oil and gas.
If Le Pen and the AfD win, that would compound Ukraine’s struggles with its allies at a time when the Trump administration is already pressuring Kyiv to compromise on its sovereignty.
“We will not be able to withstand the joint position of the European Union and the United States, and a chance to manoeuvre between Washington and Brussels will be lost,” Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kusch told Al Jazeera.

Two oil tankers exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting naval mines while attempting to transit the chokepoint via a southern route not authorized by Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Monday, as Iranian reports of such incidents have intensified in recent days.
The two tankers had attempted to pass through the route under the direct guidance of U.S. officers and with the support of U.S. military fighter jets, the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian Mehr news agency.
On Sunday and Monday alone, a total of six oil tankers caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the IRGC Navy, which added that pollution caused by the explosions had spread across the coastal areas and waters of the Strait.
"The IRGC Navy described the actions as punitive measures in response to the U.S. military's illegal blockade and violations of Iran's regulations governing the Strait of Hormuz," the Mehr news agency reported.
Moreover, the IRGC Navy warned oil tanker and oil firm owners that "the U.S.-backed southern passage through the strait had been mined, cautioning that trusting U.S. military officials and cooperating with them would put their vessels at risk."
For days, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents with tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as "unauthorized" in the Strait of Hormuz.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's top negotiator and Parliament Speaker, told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview last week that the Strait of Hormuz navigation would not return to pre-war conditions, ever.
"There are no 'free waters' [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it," the official told Al Jazeera.

items.title: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?
items.summary: The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war.
items.content:
China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin meeting in first three-way summit
The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war.
The three-way summit among the three nations is unprecedented.
"The ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first-among-equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit" for Beijing: analyst.
Russian artist Alexey Sergienko unveils his new pop art painting dubbed "Shenzhen, 26" in Saint Petersburg on November 12, 2026.
China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.
That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.
While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.
"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.
Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.
The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.
"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world , whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call . The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
China has no interest in engaging in nuclear disarmament talks until it achieves parity with the U.S. in about 10 years, said David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy.
Chances of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia 'very slim': David Roche
Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.
The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, said Roche, while Trump's political standing slides. Nvidia and the chip-smuggling issues involving a suspected Chinese spy will stay off the agenda, as Trump steers clear of thorny issues where he is unlikely to claim success.
China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.
China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.
"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."
A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.
Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.
U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

items.title: Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
items.summary: Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China efforts to dominateGet our daily political email, free app or daily news podcastAnthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope
items.content:
Anthony Albanese has told the Asean-Australia summit that the region needs friendship, mutual trust and optimism to prosper. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP
Anthony Albanese has told the Asean-Australia summit that the region needs friendship, mutual trust and optimism to prosper. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP
Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China efforts to dominate
Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast
Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.
The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.
Underlying the diplomatic swing are efforts by the federal government to avoid angering China, as the Quad leaders gather for the first time since 2024 – and after Australia joined countries, including the US and Japan, in an agreement for new protections around key AI technologies.
Designed to firm up supply chains for chips and critical minerals components, the San Francisco Declaration was crafted to promote cooperation in the face of China’s efforts to control areas of AI development.
Part of the Pax Silica international accord, officials said the agreement would help ensure Trump worked with partners to set standards in AI, rather than relying on others for leadership. Signatories include the UK, India, Israel, South Korea and Singapore.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
Albanese told the Asean-Australia summit on Monday that the region needed friendship, mutual trust, and optimism to prosper.
“At a time of global instability, the cooperation we demonstrate here will help us to confront the challenges we share at home and in our region,” he said.
Federal government sources told Guardian Australia the intense international efforts, including Albanese’s attendance at the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China at the end of the week, was about maintaining engagement with Trump in the final two years of his presidency and stopping the US from withdrawing from global leadership.
How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
Asia Society senior fellow Premesha Saha said the Quad talks would focus on critical minerals, maritime security and energy security.
“For Australia, keeping the United States engaged in the Indo-Pacific is a core strategic interest, and the Quad is one of the few settings where the president is tied into a regional agenda alongside three close partners,” Saha said.
“After a year in which Washington has been engaged elsewhere and has opened its own channel with Beijing, getting Trump to a Quad leaders’ meeting in the region matters to Australia.”
Saha said Albanese’s objectives included keeping Washington engaged in the region and building a Quad capable of delivering results, even during shifts in US policy and interest.
“Beijing will criticise it, as it always does, and will cast it as bloc politics. But I will be cautious about overstating how much this will anger China,” she said.
“The Quad isn’t a military alliance, and Washington has gone out of its way to say it isn’t an anti-China coalition.”
Jennifer Parker, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, said criticism of Albanese’s involvement in the annual international summit season was shortsighted.
“Our relationships in the region are essential to our security in an increasingly chaotic world, and our security is the backbone of our national prosperity,” she said.
“It is important for Australia to be seen on the international stage and advocate for our national interests.”
Parker disagreed that Australia was working to keep the US engaged in the Asia Pacific region.
“The US has enduring interests here, both economically and strategically. But sometimes it pays for Australia to remind them of that,” she said.
Albanese announced a new Asean-Australia digital economy program on Monday, to support AI safety and intelligence standards and digital trade standards.
He said humans must remain in control of AI, shaping the technology “rather than let it shape us”.
Albanese also held one-on-one talks with the Philippines president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
He told his Laos counterpart, Saleumxay Kommasith, that Australia remained very concerned about the deaths of backpackers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles , who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vientiane in 2024.
Albanese said Australia remained concerned about the seriousness of charges over the deaths. Investigators said they did not have enough evidence to do more because autopsies were not carried out.
Albanese called the case a “tragedy” and said it remained a serious issue in Australia.
Kommasith said the Laos government had attached importance to the case and officials were “trying our best to put an end to this by bringing those perpetrators into justice”.

Gold falls to lowest since September 2025 as Fed rate hike bets weigh
Gold falls to lowest since September 2025 as Fed rate hike bets weigh
Silver drops 2.6% to around $47.4 an ounce as stronger dollar, elevated Treasury yields pressure precious metals
İSTANBUL Gold prices fell to their lowest level since September 2025 on Monday as a stronger US dollar and elevated Treasury yields weighed on precious metals amid expectations of further Federal Reserve interest rate increases.
Gold traded at $3,855.06 an ounce, down $26.69, or 0.69% as of 0720GMT, while silver declined $1.30, or 2.66%, to $47.43 an ounce.
The latest declines brought gold's monthly losses to 6.91%, while silver dropped 16.9% over the same period.
Expectations of further US monetary tightening pressured both metals as investors assessed inflation concerns and signals from Fed policymakers.
Several Fed officials indicated that additional rate increases may be necessary, with some suggesting a larger 50-basis-point hike could be considered in December.
Market pricing pointed to a 92% probability of a quarter-point increase next month and an 8% chance of a half-point hike.
Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing assets such as gold and silver, while a stronger dollar makes dollar-denominated metals more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
Investors awaited remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh later Monday for further indications of the central bank's policy direction, alongside the release of minutes from its October meeting on Wednesday.
Silver, which fell to its lowest level in about a year, also faced pressure from weaker demand expectations linked to declining consumption in jewelry and solar cells.

items.content:
If the Stock Market Crashes, Warren Buffett Says This is the Best Move Investors Can Make
The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) has advanced 10% year to date amid remarkably strong earnings growth driven by the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out. Yet, investors have become increasingly pessimistic throughout the year, raising a familiar question: What should you do if the market takes a turn for the worse?
Warren Buffett has addressed this question repeatedly. His advice starts with accepting that steep declines are part of stock ownership. No one can reliably predict when the next crash will happen, but investors can decide in advance how they will respond.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Bearish sentiment has increased sharply throughout the year
Weekly surveys conducted by the American Association of Individual Investors (AAII) show that bearish sentiment -- the percentage of investors who expect the stock market to decline over the next six months -- increased from 27% in January to 51% in November.
Possible explanations include doubts about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom and whether the profits it generates will justify massive infrastructure spending. Midterms may have added to those concerns, as several incoming governors and members of Congress support data center restrictions, including moratoriums on construction projects.
Meanwhile, high energy prices tied to the Iran conflict and tariffs imposed by President Trump have contributed to inflation. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September, and the market expects another hike in December, according to CME Group 's FedWatch tool. Higher rates make bonds more attractive, which can pull money away from stocks.
Any of those pressures could deepen the recent sell-off. But even if the stock market recovers in the near term, the next severe downturn is inevitable. So, it makes sense to have a plan in place before it arrives.
Warren Buffett's advice is to buy good businesses when pessimism creates bargains
Stock market downturns can make selling seem like the safest move. But Warren Buffett has repeatedly explained that falling prices are actually an opportunity for patient investors to purchase stock in their favorite companies at a discount.
"Widespread fear is your friend as an investor, because it serves up bargain purchases," he wrote in his 2016 shareholder letter. That sentiment is particularly relevant today given that investors have become increasingly bearish throughout the year. That hard part is deciding where to invest your money.
Buffett answered that question in his 1996 letter. "Your goal as an investor should simply be to purchase, at a rational price, a part interest in an easily-understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher five, ten, and twenty years from now."
That quote is jam-packed with good advice. First, Buffett makes it clear that price matters. Second, investors must understand a company before buying shares. Third, investors should only consider stocks whose earnings are likely to be much higher in the future.
Drawdowns have historically been an excellent opportunity to buy stocks
The Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) recently entered correction territory , and similar downturns in the past reveal an encouraging pattern. During the last decade, the Nasdaq returned an average of 21% over the 12-month period following its first close in correction territory.
The S&P 500 is not currently in correction territory, but it has displayed a similar resilience during past downturns. Specifically, during the last decade, the S&P 500 has returned an average of 18% over the 12-month period following its first close in correction territory.
Here's the bottom line: Market downturns are part of the investing experience. But history says stocks will eventually recover and Buffett's advice provides a clear plan: Focus on understandable businesses with strong long-term growth prospects, and buy when shares trade at sensible prices.
If the stock market crashes tomorrow, investors should put that advice into action. And they should plan to hold any stocks they buy for at least five years. items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming in 2027, Warren Buffett’s Advice Makes My Next Move Clear - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming in 2027, Warren Buffett’s Advice Makes My Next Move Clear  The Motley Fool
items.content:
A 2027 crash can't be ruled out, so investors should have a plan in place ahead of time.
With a diversified portfolio, investors can insulate themselves from the worst outcomes during a crash.
Buffett’s 2013 letter advocates low costs, broad stock ownership, and spreading purchases over time.
Volatility has returned to the stock market. Since hitting a record high on Oct. 6, 2026, the Nasdaq Composite has dropped more than 10%. That leaves many investors asking a rational, if concerning, question: Is a stock market crash on the horizon?
This anxiety leads many investors to pull up stakes and retreat from the market altogether. That strategy creates a new problem: when to get back into the market.
Therefore, I would suggest that during volatile periods – like right now – investors should take a page from Warren Buffett's playbook. Namely, build an investing strategy and schedule that can withstand volatility. Here's how to do it.
First things first, investors don't need to be fortune tellers. Indeed, even if someone could accurately predict market crashes , they would still need to accurately predict market bottoms – something that is just as unlikely as predicting tops.
A better strategy accepts that negative outcomes are inevitable, but rare, and can be mitigated with some planning.
To illustrate, think of someone who enjoys spending time outdoors but wants to avoid getting soaked by the rain. They could be 100% sure to avoid the rain by canceling every outdoor activity for the next year, but that would be a massive hassle. Conversely, they could simply check the weather forecast each morning and carry an umbrella on days when the chance of rain is high.
Once investors have planned for downturns, they can focus on which investments best carry them safely through volatile periods. Here, it's best to turn directly to the Oracle of Omaha for advice.
Rather than chasing short-term market fads, Buffett has advised investors to take long-term positions in real businesses they can easily understand. That's why Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway ( BRKB -0.52% ) ( BRKA -0.66% ) has owned large stakes in companies like Coca-Cola ( KO +0.93% ) , American Express ( AXP -0.61% ) , and Moody's ( MCO -0.02% ) for decades.
By stretching the time horizon out to 10, 20, 30 years or more, recent interest rate movements, unemployment reports, and GDP forecasts all fade in importance. Over long periods, what matters most is whether a company's business model is resilient and whether its management team is guiding it properly.
To borrow a line from Buffett himself, he quipped that he looks for companies so wonderful that "an idiot can run them, because sooner or later, one will."
Once you have the right mindset and the right stocks on your watch list, it's time to talk execution. A great strategy will still fail if it's not executed properly. Therefore, it's best to write rules that can be followed – even on a bad day.
Start small. If a person can only put $10 in the market each month, it's better than nothing. Raise the contribution amount when possible. Ensure there's an emergency reserve, separate from investment funds, for unexpected bills, large purchases, and similar expenses.
Finally, remember that investing during volatile periods can be emotionally taxing. Find ways to see the bright side when the market is moving lower. If a normal monthly contribution of $100 normally buys 1 share of stock , remind yourself that during volatile periods, $100 might buy 1.5 shares. Over time, those additional shares will add up.
No one knows what 2027 holds. A stock market crash could be on the way, but that won't keep anyone from investing. Instead, stick to the investing strategy and rules laid out by one of the best to ever do it: Contribute regularly, invest in great companies, and play the long game.
Over time, that strategy made Warren Buffett one of the wealthiest people on the planet, and it can no doubt help many others achieve their financial goals – regardless of whether a stock market crash is on the horizon.

items.title: Trump’s Hormuz squeeze has Iran strangled — now slam its back door, too - New York Post
items.summary: Trump’s Hormuz squeeze has Iran strangled — now slam its back door, too  New York Post
items.content:
Cargo trucks halted at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing at the border between Pakistan and Iran during a temporary suspension of trade on Oct. 21, 2026.
America no longer needs a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump proclaimed last week.
“We’ve got their money . . . and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote Thursday.
He’s right about the Strait of Hormuz: Gulf oil is flowing through the passage again under US Navy escort, despite Iranian attacks on shipping — but Iran hasn’t loaded a barrel of oil onto a ship since Aug. 25.
Before the US blockade, Iran’s southern sea routes carried as much as 80% of its trade.
What still reaches Tehran comes mostly by land, across seven international borders .
Those roads have become the regime’s lifeline. It’s now time to close them.
American blockades at sea and in the air demonstrate what effective enforcement can do.
In March, the first month of the war, almost no crude oil from the Arab countries passed through Hormuz; in October, 10.3 million barrels a day did, about three-quarters of the prewar flow.
But the US Navy has bottled up Iran’s tanker fleet, and that’s inflicted real damage: In mid-October Iran sold the last of the 89 million barrels it had on tankers beyond the blockade line.
Its Chinese buyers pay a month or two after delivery, so the final payments could arrive around mid-December.
Now, a senior budget official is saying Tehran “must prepare for circumstances in which oil revenue reaches zero.”
The sky is closing too : Since Treasury sanctioned the last of Iran’s airlines in September, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan have barred them all.
China’s and Russia’s are the last major runways still open.
The roads, however, are allowing the regime to rearm and to buy time.
At least $2 billion in military supplies has reached Iran since January 2025, some of it by truck from Central Asia.
A land blockade doesn’t mean sealing 3,700 miles of frontier.
Heavy freight must pass through a limited number of official crossings, and trucks cannot carry the loads that ships do: An official at Iran’s own Chamber of Commerce has estimated that one cargo vessel equals about 2,500 trucks.
Close most crossings, inspect every truck at the rest, and Iran’s lifeline becomes a queue.
To that end, this month US Central Command established Task Force Iron Gate , charged with stopping weapons, sanctioned goods and illicit cash from crossing Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.
The goal is to make the overland route slow, expensive and payable only in the hard currency the regime no longer earns.
By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
And the plan is to have Iran’s neighbors, not American troops, enforce the blockade with their own border guards.
Three countries, Iraq, Pakistan and Turkmenistan, guard more than 60% of Iran’s land border.
But persuading them to take part in the effort has been tricky: Iraq has so far refused Washington’s request to close all but two of its crossings, and Pakistan has shuttered them intermittently.
CENTCOM needs to take action to strengthen the case for cooperation.
It must offer intelligence: The US must pledge to share data from American satellites, drones and financial investigators, so border commanders can know which trucks to open.
It must offer partnership: CENTCOM’s naval arm leads a coalition of more than 40 nations, including Iraq and Pakistan, that hunts smugglers at sea. Iron Gate should be that coalition on land.
And it must use its existing leverage: It’s hard to say no to the military force that has trained you for decades.
The US-led coalition trained and equipped Iraq’s border guards, Washington approved a $686 million upgrade of Pakistan’s F-16s last year, and CENTCOM paid for a border checkpoint on Turkmenistan’s frontier with Iran.
CENTCOM should make clear that future training, equipment and funding depend on cooperation at the Iranian border.
Treasury has sanctioned Iran’s rail and auto sectors, truck makers included.
It should back the task force by putting every freight forwarder, trucking company and inland port on notice that hauling the regime’s cargo means losing access to the dollar.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf predicted on Nov. 11 that the incoming Congress will pile political pressure on the White House.
Trump must prove him wrong. No deal has to mean no letup.
There’s no need for another major military campaign while economic pressure does the same work.
Save military force for the minelayers and missile crews that threaten ships and Americans.
Anything wider hands the regime the war it would use to hide a broken economy.
The sea is closed to the regime, and the sky is closing.
Close the roads, and it will be left alone with the 90 million Iranians it has robbed for 47 years.
Then it will have two choices: accept America’s terms, or answer to its own people.

U.S. LNG flows jumped to an all-time high this weekend as various projects ramp up production and shipments to markets in Europe and Asia that are reeling from the supply shock in the Middle East.
Pipeline flows to U.S. LNG facilities surged to a record high of 21.8 billion cubic feet on Saturday, up by 12% from this time last year, data from BloombergNEF showed on Monday.
Estimated pipeline gas flows to the Golden Pass project hit a record high this weekend, while pipeline flows to Sabine Pass soared to their highest level since April 2026, per the BloombergNEF data.
Several new U.S. projects have ramped up capacity, and existing liquefaction trains have boosted overseas shipments as Europe and Asia are competing for every spot LNG cargo not needing to transit the Strait of Hormuz.

Europe remains in a vulnerable gas supply position ahead of winter as LNG flows from the Strait of Hormuz are still way below pre-war levels and QatarEnergy has extended the force majeure on deliveries until the end of December 2026, at the very least.

European Gas Slumps on Milder Weather and Record U.S. LNG Flows
European benchmark natural gas prices slumped in Amsterdam trade early on Monday as immediate supply concerns eased with forecasters expecting milder weather in the coming days and U.S. LNG flows hitting a record high this weekend.
The front-month price at the Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) , the benchmark for Europe's gas trading, dipped by 3.3% as of 10:00 a.m. in Amsterdam on Monday, and traded at $96.85 (87.965 euros) per megawatt-hour (MWh).
That's lower than the end of last week, when Europe's gas prices posted a weekly gain of 6% as uncertainty about the Iran war returned to the energy markets following steep selloffs right after the U.S. midterm elections.
While falling from last week's highs, the European benchmark gas price is well above the price at this time last year, as storage sites across the EU are only 70% full, compared to 89% in November 2025.
Despite the lowest level of gas in storage in Europe, two bearish factors eased Europe's benchmark prices early on Monday—expectations of milder temperatures in the coming week in most of Europe, and record-high flows of piped gas to U.S. LNG facilities this weekend.
Pipeline flows to U.S. LNG facilities surged to a record high of 21.8 billion cubic feet on Saturday, up by 12% from this time last year, data from BloombergNEF showed on Monday.
Several new U.S. projects have ramped up capacity and existing liquefaction trains have boosted overseas shipments as Europe and Asia are competing for every spot LNG cargo not needing to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
Despite temporarily eased concerns, Europe remains in a vulnerable gas supply position ahead of winter as LNG flows from the Strait of Hormuz are still way below pre-war levels and QatarEnergy has extended the force majeure on deliveries until the end of December 2026, at the very least.

items.title: Elon Musk joins 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign to reinstate the ex-Nvidia boss
items.summary: A number of tech figures want the board of the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
items.content:
Image caption, SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang
Allies of Jensen Huang are trying to rally support for the former Nvidia boss to get his job back after resigning last week over a scandal involving extramarital affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, are among those backing a campaign to get the AI chip giant's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after the emergence of two affairs, one of whom was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.
An open letter calling for Nvidia's board to give Huang his job back while an internal probe is conducted has received more than 175,000 signatures, including Musk and Sweeney, according to a website named "Stand with Jensen".
The campaign group said it is made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.
"We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests," the letter said.
Allies of the ex-Nvidia boss wrote they were "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, this time allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times. , external
The newspaper quoted one ally saying that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being convened to lobby for the former Nvidia boss's reinstatement.
A representative for Jensen Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
While President Donald Trump recently spoke in glowing terms about Huang , the scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The former Nvidia boss has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China .
The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while the Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost," he posted on X. , external
He later added: "If Jensen gave me his word about compute delivery or I asked for components to be accelerated, he always came through."
If Huang was reinstated, it would face scrutiny from Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at Nvidia's helm.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Share USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume? on social media
US Navy aircraft sit on the flight deck on board the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt [File: Michelle Bir/AFP]
The United States has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as diplomatic efforts to permanently end the US-Israel war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled.
On Monday, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the Middle East. The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility.

The US and Iran entered into a two-week ceasefire in April and later announced a broader memorandum of understanding in June, which collapsed in early July.
Since then, mediators from Pakistan and Qatar have been trying to prevent a return to the full-scale exchange of attacks between the US and Iran that also badly affected the broader Gulf region in March.
Last week, US President Donald Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. But he noted the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.
Does the deployment of another aircraft carrier to the region mean the US-Israel war on Iran is going to resume?
Named after the 26th US president, Theodore Roosevelt, the vessel is a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.
Commissioned by the US Navy in 1986, the ship carries more than 5,000 personnel and a full air wing of more than 60 aircraft, including F-18s, the twin-engine, supersonic, all-weather multi-role fighter planes.
According to the US Navy, the warship is tasked with “conducting carrier air warfare operations and assisting in the planning, control, coordination and integration of air wing squadrons in support of carrier air warfare”.
Besides combat operations, the carrier also replenishes ships at sea and rescues people, including refugees, at sea.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt has performed combat and humanitarian missions since it was commissioned. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, it was deployed to the Mediterranean and the Red Sea for combat operations. In 2003, it also supported US strikes during the Iraq War.
It was also deployed in the Asia Pacific region from 2020-21 for military exercises with India, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia.
In October, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had left its San Diego base in September, bound for the Middle East. According to another official, it arrived in the Middle East on November 15 .
But the Pentagon and CENTCOM, which oversees military operations in the region, have not formally confirmed the carrier’s arrival.
(Al Jazeera) What is the state of US deployment in the region?
The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East brings the total number of US aircraft carrier strike groups operating in the region to three. The USS George Washington and the USS George HW Bush are the other two aircraft carriers currently deployed there.
Last month, a US official told Al Jazeera that the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG), carrying more than 2,000 Marines, had also followed the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East. The Wall Street Journal reported that the strike group and naval deployments could involve an additional 9,000 to 10,000 US soldiers in total, including sailors and Marines assigned to the carrier strike group and other ships. However, the US military is yet to confirm these deployments.
The US has had troops and military assets stationed at bases in the Middle East for decades. Of these, eight are permanent bases, located in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. As of mid-2025, there were 40,000 to 50,000 US soldiers stationed in and around the Middle East, including personnel at large, permanent bases and smaller forward sites across the region.
According to open-source intelligence analysts and military flight-tracking data, the US has deployed more than 120 aircraft to the region since early February, before the war on Iran began. That is the biggest surge in US airpower in the Middle East since the Iraq War.
Reported deployments include E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft, F-35 stealth strike fighters and F-22 air superiority jets, alongside F-15s and F-16s. In March, the Pentagon also ordered additional US forces  to the Gulf.
The reinforcements consisted of three distinct formations.
The first was the Tripoli ARG, centred around the America-class assault ship USS Tripoli and the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU).
The second was the Boxer ARG, built around the Wasp-class assault ship USS Boxer and the 11th MEU, based in southern California in the US.
Together, these two Marine groups have added 4,500 Marines and sailors in the region.
The third was a contingent of about 2,000 soldiers from the 82nd Airborne Division’s Immediate Response Force, based at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The airborne infantry division is focused on parachute assaults.
In total, nearly 7,000 additional soldiers have already been deployed to the Middle East since the US-Israel war on Iran began.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, has said the country “will not wait for the US to attack first”.
“The US may be seeking to buy time by abusing diplomacy, in order to prepare the ground for another attack,” he said.
Speaking to state TV in a video released by Iran’s Fars news agency, Gharibabadi warned, “Iran is not Cuba that you can blockade, nor is it Venezuela that you can force to surrender.”
He said US forces “have had no success with either an air blockade or a land blockade” in Iran so far, while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is currently producing missiles with “new ranges”.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for stronger regional energy cooperation, warning US attacks threaten stability across the Middle East.
“Given the increasing impact of US and Israeli aggression on the region’s energy security, strengthening energy cooperation has become an urgent and strategic necessity,” Araghchi said at a meeting of foreign ministers of the Economic Cooperation Organization in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Monday.
“Our region needs not only an independent security framework but also a regional, reliable and sustainable energy mechanism to safeguard energy flows, ensure stable energy supplies, reduce vulnerabilities from external factors, and increase our collective resilience to geopolitical shocks and disruptions,” the IRNA news agency quoted him as saying.
What has the US government said on resuming the war?
The Trump administration has appeared increasingly divided on how to proceed with Iran, since the Republican Party suffered heavy losses in this month’s US midterm elections.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran was proving effective, so a resumption of large-scale military operations was likely unnecessary. “The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.
But Trump has given mixed messages about his plans for the war.
Last week, after a meeting at the White House with Qatar’s prime minister, Trump stated on Truth Social and in a surprise briefing that there was “positive momentum” towards ending the conflict and that a resumption of strikes was “quite unlikely”, declaring the US-Israel war on Iran “effectively over”, militarily.
Still, Trump insisted that the US economic pressure campaign against Iran would stay in place, including a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and a more recent task force aimed at cutting off Iran’s trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.
Meanwhile, Iran’s conditions to end the war include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.
Iranian officials have in recent days underlined that Tehran would not accept the current status quo of “no war, no peace”.
Trump, on his part, has indicated that he is running out of patience with Iran as diplomacy stutters. Last week, the US president said he had told his country’s lead negotiator, Vice President JD Vance, “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”
“Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Ali Vaez, the International Crisis Group’s Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa, told Al Jazeera that both sides are caught in a perilous game of chicken, convinced that striking first may be safer than waiting to be struck.
“The danger is that their efforts to deter another war could inadvertently ignite one that neither can win, contain or easily end,” he said.
Diplomatic efforts to stop attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz also remain stalled.
In an interview with Al Jazeera last week, Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said that Tehran wanted to move beyond a state of “no war, no peace”.
Ghalibaf said Iran had conveyed seven conditions for a deal through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official US response. The conditions he outlined included lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, has tightened sanctions and maintained the blockade on Iranian ports.
“Diplomacy still has a pulse, but it is suffocating under the weight of mutual mistrust and maximalist demands. Unless both sides find a face-saving exit, negotiations risk becoming little more than an intermission between successive rounds of warfare,” Vaez said.
The main issues in the Iran war now are those of sequencing and leverage, according to Rashid al-Mohanadi, vice president at the Center for International Policy Research. He told Al Jazeera that “who does what, when, and how” will determine a potential end of the conflict.
Al-Mohanadi added that the region is clearly against a return to full-scale war, given that regional powers are “leading on the mediation”.
But he warned that the war’s main protagonists appear to have divergent perceptions over their leverage.
“The Iranians perceive they have more leverage. The Americans perceive they have more,” al-Mohanadi said. “When you have a situation like that, reaching a diplomatic end is quite difficult.”

Ukraine fires 1,336 drones into Russia in one of war's largest attacks, Moscow says
The attack appears to be one of the largest-ever overnight barrages by Kyiv.
LONDON -- Russia's Defense Ministry on Monday reported one of the largest Ukrainian overnight drone attacks of the war to date, with Moscow's forces claiming the shooting down of 1,336 Ukrainian craft on Sunday night and Monday morning.
The attack appears to be one of the largest-ever overnight barrages reported by the Russian Defense Ministry, according to ministry statements analyzed by ABC News. The ministry's figures cannot be independently verified.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov described the attack as "massive." He told reporters on Monday morning, "Our air defense systems continue to operate very effectively," adding, "The system is functioning, although, unfortunately, no system in the world can provide a 100% guarantee."
The attack comes as President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet later this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

Moscow was among the main targets of the attack, according to officials in the capital. Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in posts to Telegram that around 600 drones were launched toward the city in the latest barrage. Most were destroyed far from the capital, Sobyanin said, with 191 craft downed on approach to Moscow.
Elsewhere, reports indicated Ukrainian drone attacks in areas home to major oil refineries in the Rostov and Krasnodar Krai regions in the southwest of the country.

In Krasnodar, six people were injured when drone debris fell on a home, regional authorities said. A fire was also reported in the village of Ilsky, which is home to a large oil refinery that has previously been targeted by Ukrainian drones.
Ukraine's General Staff said in a statement that its drones hit the Ilsky refinery, which it said is "one of the largest oil refineries in southern Russia, with a capacity to process approximately 6.6 million metric tons of crude oil per year."
"Its location in the south makes the plant particularly important to the military: from here, fuel has the shortest route to Russian forces on the front lines and in occupied Crimea," the General Staff added.
The General Staff said that drones also hit the "Flash Energy LLC oil depot in the city of Azov, Rostov Oblast," describing the refinery as another that is key for frontline Russian logistics.

The Crimean Bridge -- which spans the Kerch Strait connecting Krasnodar Krai in Russia to occupied Crimea -- was also attacked, according to the Moscow-appointed head of occupied Crimea. Sergey Aksenov said in a post to Telegram that traffic on the bridge would be restricted until midday.

Russia's federal air transport agency, Rosaviatsiya, reported significant disruptions all across western Russia. Two of Moscow's four international airports -- Vnukovo and Sheremetyevo -- were among those put under temporary flight restrictions amid the latest attacks.
Airports in Yaroslavl, Kaluga, Nizhny Novgorod, Krasnodar and Sochi also faced restrictions, Rosaviatsiya said.
Russia also continued its long-range strike campaign overnight. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 158 drones, of which 77 were jet-powered, into the country on Sunday night into Monday morning. Defenders downed or suppressed 131 drones, 55 of which were jet-powered, the air force said. Impacts were recorded across 19 locations, it added.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service said in posts to Telegram that the central city of Dnipro was among the targets, where one person was killed and 10 others were injured.

A round of shuttle diplomacy by Trump's peace envoys -- Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff -- last week saw trilateral U.S.-Ukraine-Russia talks held in Abu Dhabi, but without any apparent diplomatic breakthrough.
Putin and his negotiating teams have shown no willingness to abandon maximalist war goals that would bar Ukraine from NATO membership, cap the size and capability of Kyiv's armed forces and force Ukrainian troops to surrender territory in the east of the country that Moscow's troops have been unable to take by force.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, is calling for a ceasefire along the current contact line -- a proposal repeatedly rebuffed by the Kremlin -- with talks on a final settlement to follow.

US Stock Futures Decline Ahead of Nvidia Earnings as Investors Await Federal Reserve Signals: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Nasdaq sign on building ©Adobe Stock Images US stock index futures were mostly lower on Monday as investors prepared for Nvidia's quarterly earnings announcement, further developments in the artificial intelligence sector and a series of economic releases and Federal Reserve communications.
At 03:47 ET (08:47 GMT), S&P 500 futures were down 15 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures declined 191 points, or 0.7%. Dow Jones futures were broadly unchanged.
Wall Street's main indices ended Friday's session with mixed performances following a volatile week for technology shares, influenced partly by the departure of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) Chief Executive Jensen Huang.
Huang's exit followed allegations concerning his personal relationships, including reported links to an individual suspected of involvement in Chinese intelligence activities. The allegations have raised questions about corporate governance and the company's leadership arrangements.
Reports over the weekend indicated that Huang had discussed the possibility of returning to the company as chief executive. However, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly encouraged Nvidia to appoint an external candidate.
Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, is serving as interim chief executive while the board conducts a search for a permanent replacement.
Separately, questions have emerged about whether Chinese companies could access Nvidia's advanced semiconductors through data centres in Southeast Asia, potentially circumventing US export restrictions.
Nvidia is scheduled to publish its quarterly financial results after the US market closes on Tuesday, with investors expected to examine the company's revenue outlook and its financial relationships with customers.
Analysts at Vital Knowledge said Nvidia would face particular scrutiny over its projection for revenue growth of 70% in the next financial year.
The analysts described near-term expectations as "somewhat sanguine", reflecting market assumptions that the company would reaffirm its guidance.
However, they cautioned that any increase in Nvidia's share price following the announcement could encounter selling pressure.
The analysts wrote: "It seems like any post-earnings rally will be met with a wave of selling as sentiment has turned quite cautious on the medium and long-term post-Jensen outlook for the company amid concerns it will be forced to dial back financial support for customers while facing more stringent export rules from the White House."
Attention is also turning towards the anticipated initial public offering of artificial intelligence company Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT).
The developer of the Claude chatbot is expected to complete its investor roadshow on Wednesday, ahead of a potential transaction valued at approximately $64 billion.
Reports indicate that the proposed offering has attracted substantial investor interest, although final pricing and transaction details have yet to be confirmed.
US Administration Reportedly Preparing AI National Champions Initiative
The Trump administration is preparing to designate more than two dozen US technology companies as artificial intelligence "national champions", according to a report published by The Wall Street Journal on Sunday.
The companies reportedly under consideration include Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT).
The initiative is intended to support US technology companies seeking to expand internationally and compete with Chinese businesses.
According to the report, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick could announce the programme within a week, although the timing remains subject to change.
Companies receiving the designation could benefit from accelerated export licensing procedures, government assistance for international operations and access to federal financing.
The proposed framework would also facilitate the sale of combined US technology offerings, including semiconductors, artificial intelligence models and related infrastructure, to foreign governments and commercial customers.
The programme has been presented as part of efforts to strengthen the international position of US technology companies against competitors including Huawei Technologies.
Federal Reserve Communications and Economic Data Awaited
Investors are also preparing for several US economic releases, including October retail sales and industrial production figures, alongside the minutes of the Federal Reserve's previous monetary policy meeting.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is scheduled to moderate a panel discussion in San Francisco on Monday, focusing on economic productivity, employment and the implications of artificial intelligence.
According to analysts at Deutsche Bank, the discussion is expected to address research conducted by a Federal Reserve task force examining productivity and labour market developments.
The analysts stated: "Our economists' baseline is that the task force will focus primarily on AI's potential to lift productivity and sustain strong growth without necessarily generating the same degree of inflation pressure, although possible disruption to hiring and implications for r-star could also feature."
The term "r-star" refers to the theoretical neutral interest rate at which economic activity can remain close to its potential without generating sustained inflationary or deflationary pressure.
Investors will also assess any indications regarding the Federal Reserve's December interest rate decision.
Comments from Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller last week contributed to market speculation about the possibility of a 50-basis-point rate increase.
Warsh has previously expressed reluctance to provide explicit guidance on future interest rate decisions.
Crude oil prices fluctuated on Monday as investors monitored developments in the Middle East and the potential implications for regional energy supplies.
Tensions remained elevated following the arrival of a third US aircraft carrier in the region over the weekend and reports of another attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran warned that it could launch a pre-emptive strike rather than wait for a US military attack.
Reports also indicated that Tehran had carried out drone attacks against a US military installation in Bahrain, while Iran-backed Houthi forces had made territorial gains against Saudi-backed groups in Yemen.
Despite concerns about possible supply disruptions, indications of improving regional oil availability contributed to mixed movements in crude prices.
Brent crude futures were last trading 0.5% lower at $95.36 per barrel.

Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.
Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.
Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.
Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.
“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”
In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected secret Iranian missile sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.
His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

Treasury yields fall as investors await comments from Fed Chair Warsh
NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 09: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange
Michael M. Santiago | Getty Images News | Getty Images
Treasury yields inched lower on Monday after facing upward pressure last week, as investors awaited comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh later in the session.
The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, loans and credit card debt — was down more than 2 basis points at 5.131%, having reached a high of 5.174% on Friday before easing to 5.143%.
The 2-year Treasury note yield , usually more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was more than 2 basis points lower at 4.848%. The 30-year Treasury bond yield was at 5.462%, down by more than 1 basis point.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Warsh is set to speak later on Monday on the impact of technology on productivity and jobs. His comments will come after data last week showed the producer price index , a measure of wholesale prices, was up by less than expected in October. But the index is at its highest level in nearly four years, and expectations that cost pressure could be passed on to consumers, and further fuel inflation, intensified pressure on Treasurys last week.
Retail sales, housing starts and jobless claims will be in focus this week, as inflation remains a concern.
Traders expect new retail sales figures to show growth of 0.6% for October, slightly lower than September's 0.8% rise. September's data was in large part due to a 6.4% increase in gasoline sales off the back of higher prices.
The Federal Reserve's minutes from its October meeting, where it left rates unchanged, will be released Wednesday. Markets have largely priced in a quarter percentage point hike in December, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

items.content:
4 High-Yield Energy Stocks That Get Paid to Move Oil and Gas
Published November 16, 2026, 9:17am ET · 5 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Pipelines work like toll roads. Producers pay to move natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), and crude oil whether prices are high or low, and the operators pass much of that cash to unitholders. Four midstream partnerships stand out right now because they pair large distributions with multi-year growth backlogs in the Permian and Marcellus. The safest of the group, Enterprise Products Partners ( NYSE:EPD | EPD Price Prediction ), covered its latest payout 1.9x [ 1 ] with distributable cash flow, and it still has $6.3B of growth projects under construction.
Enterprise Products, MPLX ( NYSE:MPLX ) and Energy Transfer ( NYSE:ET ) are master limited partnerships (MLPs), and so is the fourth pick, Western Midstream Partners ( NYSE:WES ). Investors own units and receive distributions rather than dividends. A publicly traded partnership avoids corporate tax treatment only if 90% or more of its gross income consists of qualifying income [ 2 ] (26 U.S.C. § 7704(c)(2)), which pipeline fees typically satisfy.
Tax form: unitholders receive a Schedule K-1 (Form 1065), Partner's Share of Income, Deductions, Credits, etc., instead of a Form 1099-DIV. K-1s often arrive later than 1099s.
Return of capital: much of each distribution is often treated as a return of capital. That portion reduces your cost basis instead of being taxed in the year you receive it, which moves more of the tax bill to the year you sell.
IRA complications: a tax-exempt account must include its share (whether or not distributed) of the gross income of the partnership from such unrelated trade or business [ 3 ] when it calculates unrelated business taxable income (26 U.S.C. § 512(c)(1)). Large MLP positions inside an IRA can trigger tax filings within the account itself.
Enterprise Products Partners: Fortress Coverage Behind a 5.9% Yield
Yield: Enterprise pays $0.56 per unit each quarter, or $2.24 annualized. The result is a high-yield 5.9% at $38.29.
Distribution safety: This is the strongest balance sheet in the group. Third-quarter distributable cash flow rose 27% [ 1 ] year over year to about $2.3B, covering the payout 1.9x and leaving $1.1B to reinvest. Net leverage is 2.9x [ 4 ] , inside a target of 2.7x to 3.25x, and about 96% of debt is fixed rate over the trailing 12 months; distributions plus $437 million [ 4 ] of buybacks used just 54% of adjusted cash flow from operations. The distribution history shows the quarterly payout climbing every year from $0.445 in 2020 to today's $0.56, and the latest payout is up 2.8% [ 4 ] from a year earlier.
Bull case: Permian processing volumes hit a record 4.6 Bcf per day [ 4 ] , up 12%. Management raised its 2025 to 2030 forecast for Permian wet gas and NGL production growth to 34% [ 4 ] from 23%. A 300 MBPD [ 1 ] Houston Ship Channel LPG expansion and the Athena processing plant are both due in the fourth quarter. An Enterprise executive said of the export expansion: "It is full. We have contracted it." [ 4 ]
Risk: Growth looks set to slow. Co-CEO Randy Fowler warned that "2027 may be more modest compared to what we're going to wind up reporting for 2026," [ 4 ] and lower Midland Basin processing margins and hedging losses remain swing factors.
Yield: MPLX raised its quarterly distribution to $1.2111, or $4.8444 annualized. That's an ultra-high yield of 8.5% at $57.25.
Distribution safety: Distributable cash flow of $1.54B covered the new payout 1.3x, and leverage is 3.8x against a 4.0x target. The raise checks out against the history: the quarterly payout went from $0.85 to $0.9565 in 2024, to $1.0765 in 2025, and to $1.2111 now. That's the third consecutive year of 12.5% raises.
Bull case: More than 90% of the $2.9B organic growth budget goes to Permian and Marcellus natural gas and NGL infrastructure, with management expecting mid-teens returns. Adjusted EBITDA rose 5.3% to $1.86B, gathering throughput rose 4% to 7,216 MMcf/d, and management guides to 12.5% distribution growth through 2027. The BANGL expansion and Blackcomb Pipeline are scheduled for Q4 2026.
Risk: Much of MPLX's cash flow depends on commercial agreements with its sponsor, Marathon Petroleum ( NYSE:MPC ). At 1.3x, coverage is lower than at Enterprise, and leverage is edging up while the multi-year project scheduled is being built.
Energy Transfer: 20 Straight Raises and Data Center Gas Demand
Yield: Energy Transfer pays $0.3425 [ 5 ] per unit quarterly, or $1.372 annualized. That's an ultra-high-yield 7.1% at $19.42.
Distribution safety: Third-quarter distributable cash flow attributable to partners rose to about $2.5 billion [ 6 ] from $1.9 billion, and adjusted EBITDA rose 31% [ 5 ] to $5.03B. The latest payout was the 20th consecutive quarterly increase [ 5 ] , up 3% from a year ago. Long-term holders will remember that the history also shows a cut from $0.305 to $0.1525 in 2020. The payout has since moved back above its pre-cut level.
Bull case: Management raised 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $19.7B-$19.9B [ 5 ] from $18.8B-$19.1B. Phase I of the Hugh Brinson Pipeline entered service with 1.5 Bcf per day [ 6 ] of capacity, and Phase II should take it above 2.3 Bcf per day in the first quarter of 2027. Since early 2025, Energy Transfer has signed more than 9.5 million MMBtu per day [ 6 ] of agreements with hyperscalers, data centers, and power plants. The pending Vaquero Midstream deal is priced at about 8.5x [ 6 ] estimated 2027 EBITDA.
Risk: Spending is heavy. Growth capex is about $7B [ 5 ] for 2027, which the CFO called "the high watermark." [ 6 ] Third-quarter GAAP EPS of $0.33 missed expectations of $0.4072, weighed down by $379M of unrealized hedging losses.
Western Midstream Partners: Biggest Yield, Most Homework
Yield: Western Midstream pays $0.93 per unit quarterly, or $3.72 annualized. That's an ultra-high-yield 8.8% at $42.24, the highest payout of the four.
Distribution safety: CEO Oscar Brown put coverage at "roughly 1.4 or something like that." Pro forma net leverage is about 3.2x [ 7 ] , and liquidity is about $1.8 billion. Third-quarter distributable cash flow was $512 million [ 7 ] , and 2026 free cash flow guidance holds at $1.1 billion to $1.3 billion. The payout rose from $0.875 to $0.91 in 2025 and to $0.93 in 2026. It has been flat for three quarters, and the board typically decides on raises in February.
Bull case: Delaware Basin gas throughput hit a record 2.6 Bcf/d [ 8 ] , up 20% sequentially, after the Brazos Delaware II acquisition. Management expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA to land above the center of $2.75B-$2.95B [ 8 ] . The Pathfinder water pipeline is about a 10% [ 7 ] return asset on its anchor commitment alone, and management hopes to move it toward 20%-plus as volumes fill. Brown said that the "yield today is something like 8.75%, which seems a little peppy given the strong outlook in the business." [ 7 ]
Risk: Third-quarter EPS of $0.78 [ 8 ] missed expectations of $0.9094. Gas gross margin per Mcf fell to $1.25 [ 8 ] from $1.35, free cash flow fell 38.6% year over year, and capex is running slightly above the top of guidance.
All four partnerships are collecting fees on rising Permian and Marcellus gas and NGL volumes, and each covers its payout with distributable cash flow. Enterprise offers the most safety, MPLX the clearest distribution growth, Energy Transfer the strongest data center play, and Western Midstream the biggest current check. In early 2027, keep an eye on Western Midstream's February distribution decision, Energy Transfer's Hugh Brinson Phase II start-up, and how fast Enterprise fills its expanded LPG dock.

Gold Falls Below $3,900 as Stronger Dollar and Fed Rate Expectations Pressure Precious Metals
Fine gold ©Hamiltonleen Gold prices extended their decline on Monday, remaining below $3,900 per ounce as a firmer US dollar and expectations of further interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve weighed on precious metals.
At 00:10 ET (05:10 GMT), spot gold (XAU/USD) fell 0.4% to $3,868.88 per ounce, while gold futures declined 0.3% to $3,871.92.
Other precious metals also recorded losses. Spot silver (XAG/USD) dropped 2.1% to $47.7430 per ounce, while platinum (XPT/USD) declined 1.3% to $1,473.49.
Spot palladium (XPD/USD) fell 1.4% to $985.81, while palladium futures decreased 1.6% to $984.25.
Meanwhile, the US Dollar Index advanced 0.03% to 103.44, adding pressure to dollar-denominated commodities.
Gold had already fallen 4.5% during the previous week, reaching its lowest level in more than a year as higher oil prices contributed to inflation concerns and expectations that US borrowing costs would remain elevated.
US Inflation Data Reinforces Expectations of Further Rate Increases
Recent US economic data has strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue tightening monetary policy.
Producer prices accelerated in October, recording their largest annual increase in four years. The figures added to concerns about persistent inflation and supported expectations of another interest rate increase at the Federal Reserve's December meeting.
Several central bank officials have also indicated that further action may be necessary to bring inflation under control.
Kansas City Federal Reserve President Jeff Schmid said on Sunday that inflation was still "running too hot" and that policymakers had "some work to do" to address continuing price pressures.
Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Friday that inflation had become the main consideration in his monetary policy assessment, with economic growth continuing and labour market conditions showing signs of stabilisation.
His comments suggested support for additional interest rate increases.
Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins also indicated that tighter monetary policy could be required, suggesting that borrowing costs might need to rise further than she had previously expected.

According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders are pricing in a 94% probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting.
The remaining 6% probability is assigned to a larger increase of 50 basis points.
Some investors also anticipate that the central bank could continue raising borrowing costs beyond December if inflation remains elevated.
Attention will now turn to Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who is scheduled to speak later on Monday.
Investors will also examine the minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting, due for publication on Wednesday, for further indications about the direction of monetary policy.
Geopolitical developments in the Middle East also remained under scrutiny following reports of further military activity involving Iran and regional forces.
On Sunday, Saudi-backed forces reportedly retreated during fighting against Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Separately, Iran was reported to have launched drone attacks against US military bases in Bahrain.
The developments added to uncertainty surrounding regional security and energy markets, although expectations of higher US interest rates and dollar strength remained the principal factors affecting gold prices during Monday's trading.
