Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda items, but many hope world’s three biggest nuclear powers will talk about denuclearisation
The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.
The confirmation of Thursday’s first-of-their-kind trilateral talks, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit , cements Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
The topics up for discussion are far from clear but many – including the UN secretary general – are hoping that denuclearisation will be discussed between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.
In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.
“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said the foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia , and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said “the signficance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate”.
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”.
People gather to watch a light show on buildings in Shenzhen, the host city for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Photograph: Wang Zhao/AFP/Getty Images However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.
Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.
Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict, and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.
In contrast, as feared by Kyiv, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine might not come up at all, despite Putin reportedly wanting it to.
US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
For Xi, “much of the political benefit” will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC.
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.
Sari Arho Havrén, from the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

As of 08:36 p.m. EST, Dow futures declined 0.11%, while the S&P 500 futures were down 0.22% and Nasdaq-100 futures fell 0.58%.
On Friday, the three U.S. benchmark indexes posted a mixed close amid a volatile week on Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite led the decline, shedding more than 200 points to close 0.91% lower. The S&P 500 lost 0.40% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.10%.
Despite the volatility from Nvidia's leadership upheaval, U.S. benchmark indexes ended the week in the green. The Nasdaq, S&P 500 and Dow all closed more than 2% higher.
Last week, markets contended with uncertainty at AI darling Nvidia as the CEO's departure left the company in the lurch. The chipmaker's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in as the interim CEO even as the board continues to scour for a full-time replacement both internally and externally.
However, many on Wall Street have expressed an interest in Huang returning to the helm of the company. Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said that the odds of Huang returning are increasing. In a post on X, he said, "I now put the odds Jensen returns at 51%. On Friday I had it at 10%. Kalshi currently has it at 9%."
He outlined two reasons for his increased odds: "1. The bring back Jensen movement is gaining momentum. 2. Jensen "resigning" was facade, given the Board forced his hand. But that distinction between "resigning" and getting fired is key because it gives the Board air cover that they never let him go and therefore could welcome him back."
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and several other prominent tech founders and investors, including more than 150,000 petition signatories, are urging the company to reinstate Huang, citing his industry relationships and strategic importance.
Musk said in a post on X over the weekend, "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Meanwhile, Nvidia said last week that it remains on track to post its third-quarter results under interim CEO Kress on Nov. 17. Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives, reportedly said in a note that the main task at hand for Kress is to restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter," he wrote, as per CNBC.
In a post on X, Ives said that he was not confident about Huang returning to the company. "We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO. It's about moving forward for Nvidia and it starts Tuesday with earnings as Colette leads NVDA ahead (for now)."
Another major catalyst for markets this week is Claude-market Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is looking at a valuation of about $1.4 trillion.
Ryan Detrick, CMT, Chief Market Strategist at Carson Group, warned in a post on X, "With Anthropic's IPO likely later this week, good time to remember that huge pops are normal on Day 1, but so are enormous drawdowns during that first year."
On the geopolitical front, U.S. President Donald Trump has signalled that America would refrain from pursuing further attacks on Iran. However, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran's deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, said over the weekend that Tehran "will not wait for the U.S. to attack first" and suggested that Washington might be buying time through diplomacy to prepare for another attack.

Cantwell calls on Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China
Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the ranking member on the Senate commerce panel, is urging Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to use his authority to stop the flow of advanced AI chips to companies with ties to China.
Lutnick has drawn scrutiny since news broke about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and reports that the commerce secretary slow-walked attempts to crack down on the sale of restricted chips to China.
Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the Senate banking committee, has called Lutnick to testify before Congress in December.
Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) speaks during a press conference following the weekly policy luncheon, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., June 3, 2025.
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit
The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing
Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation
Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe
Howard Lutnick's sons' Nvidia ties amid Huang China spy scandal
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

The companies' orders are expected to keep Google's older v8 chips in heavy use even as Google shifts its own computing expansion toward v9, Kuo said.
That note highlights that custom chip demand will continue climbing, despite widespread expectations that AI spending will peak in 2028. Kuo's estimates put shipments at 8–9 million units in 2027, 14–15 million in 2028 and 16–18 million in 2029, according to Kuo.

Chip stocks were pulling Wall Street lower before the opening bell, and the Nasdaq-100 was taking most of the hit. The Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, was down 1% in premarket trading. The Dow's ETF proxy was about flat. Huang stepped down as CEO and left the board Thursday. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim chief executive, according to CNBC. Chip stocks fell again Friday, and that weakness spread overnight to South Korea, Shanghai and Japan, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The selling is concentrated in tech. QQQ is down 8% over the past month, while DIA is up 1%. In the latest sector results, technology fell about 2% and consumer staples rose about 1%.

items.title: NATO member Estonia to close Russia border after attempted 'sabotage' of drone maker
items.summary: Estonia says closing the crossings would help curb hostile activity and sanctions circumvention.
items.content:
NATO: Estonia to close border with Russia after attack on drone maker
Estonia says it will shut border crossings with Russia after blaming Moscow for an attempted arson attack on a drone maker.
Tallinn says the attack fits Russia's wider hybrid campaign against NATO states.
The move adds to fears Russia is escalating pressure on Europe after nearly five years of war against Ukraine.
A woman walks to Russia from Estonia at the Luhamaa border crossing on October 3, 2025 in Luhamaa, Estonia.
NATO member Estonia says it is preparing to close road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1, as it blames Moscow for an attempted "sabotage" of one of its defense companies.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that Russia's military intelligence service GRU had ordered an arson attack against Estonian drone maker Threod Systems in the early hours of Saturday morning.
Authorities said the attempted attack did not cause significant damage and eight people were detained in connection with it.
Estonia, which shares a 294-kilometer (183-mile) border with Russia, said closing the crossings would help to reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activities against it and mitigate risks related to sanctions circumvention.
Tallinn has frequently raised the alarm over sabotage attacks against NATO countries that have been supporting Ukraine since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
"This weekend's attempted sabotage against an Estonian defence company, attributed by our security authorities to Russia's GRU, is yet another reminder that Russia's hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Sunday via social media.
"Estonia is preparing to close its road border crossings with Russia in response. Hostile actions must have consequences."
A coat of arms of the Estonian police and the Estonian flag are displayed on the uniform of an Estonian policeman standing on the border bridge from the Estonian city of Narva to Russia.
Tsahkna said he had informed his Finnish, Lithuanian and Latvian counterparts of the decision.
Russia's foreign ministry said it would assess Estonia's plans to close its border crossings, adding that if these plans were to come into force, it would be seen as "yet another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia," according to state news agency Tass .
It did not directly comment on the accusation that Moscow is responsible for the attack on Threod Systems.
"Estonia is building walls. Many countries, as history shows, have built walls that have brought no good to their creators," Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov said Monday, according to comments reported by Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti .
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack was part of Russia's broader "hybrid war" against Europe.
"We will not be intimidated. Estonia is preparing for the possibility of closing its border with Russia to reduce the risks to our people and national security," Michal said Sunday via social media.
The latest incident follows an arson attack in mid-August against Milrem Robotics, an Estonian defense company that supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles. Estonian authorities later blamed Russia for the attack. Moscow denied the allegation.
European security officials and lawmakers have previously warned about Russia's hybrid warfare. In September, Danish intelligence officials said Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.

items.title: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
items.summary: The poet, writer and diplomat died in Europe in 1974 having been forced to leave his native country.
items.content:
Image caption, The urn was placed in soil brought from different parts of Guatemala in a ceremony honouring the long-exiled poet, author and diplomat
By Vanessa BuschschlÃ¼ter Latin America online editor
The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ãngel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.
His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.
Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.
The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.
His son, whose name is also Miguel Ãngel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies."
Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology.
Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.
Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations.
Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises.
Image caption, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta MenchÃº (centre) attended a ceremony to welcome the ashes of Asturias back to Guatemala alongside the writer's son (right)
Between 1944 and 1954, a period known as "Guatemala's 10 Years of Spring", he served in several diplomatic posts in Central and South America and continued writing.
But when the democratically elected Guatemalan President Jacobo Ãrbenz GuzmÃ¡n was deposed in a CIA-backed coup in 1954, Asturias was stripped of his Guatemalan citizenship, his books were banned and he had to go into exile.
At Sunday's burial ceremony, Asturias's son said that the writer had "always wanted to be in Guatemala" but "political conditions did not allow him to".
The family only agreed to have the ashes moved from PÃ¨re Lachaise cemetery in Paris to Guatemala after the current progressive president of Guatemala, Bernardo ArÃ©valo, was elected in 2023.
ArÃ©valo praised Asturias at the interment ceremony as "our voice in the world".
"He deserved to rest in the land he named and reinvented in his pages," said ArÃ©valo, whose father Juan JosÃ© appointed Asturias to the diplomatic service when the older ArÃ©valo served as president during the 10 Year Spring.

Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
PM to meet European leaders at summit this week aiming to secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’
Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.
It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.
Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.
Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”
Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:
Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.
It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
And it passes the so-called “ Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.
“This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”
However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.
He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.
The exit clause, previously nicknamed the “Farage clause” , is designed to guard against any the cost of potentially reversing any reset on Friday should the UK’s political landscape change.
The cost of infrastructure at the borders has largely been paid for by private companies, including Eurotunnel, but French staff the food checks there, at Calais port and at Boulogne-sur-Mer, where all fish checks take place.
Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.
He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority. He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, and Ursula von der Leyen, European Commission president, at a summit last week. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Pool PA/AP
Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future
Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.
The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.
At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “ O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us! ” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin , the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.
UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent , which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.
Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.
Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.
UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police . West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.
Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance . The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.
In depth: ‘This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms’
While official discussions about the UK rejoining the EU are not on the agenda this week, there is genuine enthusiasm about the matter. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).
Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.
But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).
Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”
The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?
Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.
There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.
The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.
And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?
In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.
Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.
It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership : will the EU welcome future closeness this week?
I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back” ? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?
The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”
But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me : what else is Europe worrying about?
The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right , street protests , hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026 .
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.
There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.
Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”
Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.
Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.
Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.

Photograph: The Guardian “PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian ’s front page today.
The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.
The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror ’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT ’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.
This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald , traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US , the setting of all its games so far.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Hidde Burgmans with an accidental find in Palermo, Sicily. He has used his skills as a digital designer to create a global app for sightings of special trees. Photograph: Nadia Roeleveld Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.
Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app . “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

items.summary: 'You're going to win the war': Harry praises war veterans on surprise Ukraine visit  BBC
items.content:
'You're going to win the war': Harry praises war veterans on surprise Ukraine visit
Watch: Prince Harry meets veterans on surprise visit to Lviv
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
Prince Harry watched a wheelchair rugby match taking place inside a noise sports centre as part of his trip
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
Mykhailo Damaskin, pictured with his dog Stitch, has received experimental treatment to walk
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
Prince Harry met Kostiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted by a drone from the front
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
Injured veterans took part in a game of wheelchair rugby
Olga Rudeva, chief executive of the SuperHumans Center, said it is seeing more injured civilians than ever because of "changes to the frontlines".
"The Russians are doing double taps , they are targeting civilian infrastructure," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
As a result, "it's not only about [an] increased number of patients, it's about increased complexity of new cases."
Russia has repeatedly denied it aims for civilian targets.
Blast damage from missiles on an historic building in Lviv
At a noisy sports centre in Lviv, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Ivan Voinov, who lost a leg, has learned to dance again with his wife
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
A Banksy-style piece of street art in Lviv shows the missiles falling
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

items.title: U.S. Army Officer In Iran War Makes Damning Claim Against Trump Administration On '60 Minutes' - Yahoo News Singapore
items.summary: U.S. Army Officer In Iran War Makes Damning Claim Against Trump Administration On '60 Minutes'  Yahoo News Singapore
items.content:
Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom accused military brass of a "tactical failure"  in not protecting a logistics command post from an Iranian drone strike that killed the first six Americans in the ongoing war.
"The protection that was there was to stop car bombs and threats like that," he told " 60 Minutes " on Sunday . "There was nothing there designed to protect from an aerial attack."
Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost .
Ramsbottom's claim on national TV rebutted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's insistence that the Army Reserve's 103rd Sustainment Command center at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait ― just 65 miles from Iran ― was "fortified" but got victimized by a "once in a while" "squirter."
Before the episode ran, Ramsbottom filed a whistleblower report to the House and Senate armed services committees, alleging that concerns about drones fell on deaf ears at the Pentagon, CNN reported .
Politics: Defiant Pete Hegseth Dismisses Impeachment Push As A 'Stunt' In First Pentagon Briefing In Months
Hegseth withstood a House effort last week to launch impeachment proceedings related to the war, but Democrats likely aren't finished with their investigations into the conflict of choice started by President Donald Trump, Hegseth and Israel.
Ramsbottom said fears of drone vulnerability were forwarded to the unit commander and Maj. Gen. John Hinson. Ramsbottom said he wasn't satisfied with the response.
"I brought it up twice in various meetings, basically saying, 'Hey, I don't see how we're protected here,'" Ramsbottom told Norah O'Donnell in the segment. "He said, 'We don't have to worry about protection.'"
Ramsbottom, who was injured in the attack along with dozens of others, gave a scathing assessment of a base he said has been described as a "trailer park."
Politics: Before Trump Bombed Iran, Pentagon Slashed Teams Meant To Limit Civilian Casualties
"I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself, all the way down to my level," he said. "Yes, we did not plan this well. And this needs to be a lesson that we learn."
More than 800 Americans have been wounded and 23 have reportedly died in the war, which also has led to spikes in prices stateside and cost Trump and his party dearly in the midterm elections.
